title: Creatures Ecology and Threats
summary: Defines creature taxonomy, origin, ecology, sapience, social relationships and the difference between fauna, peoples and enemies.

blocks.text: Public project: Symphony of Justice | Internal/original name: Symphonia Iustitiae

Define the creatures of Symphony of Justice as real inhabitants of the world rather than merely units created to generate combat encounters. Every creature must have a justification within the universe:

Why does it exist?
 Where does it live?
 What does it need to survive?
 What relationship does it have with other species?
 What do societies do when they encounter it?
but its existence must not depend exclusively on the player needing something to attack.
The central rule is: The world does not generate creatures for the player. The player enters ecosystems that already existed before their arrival.

This will help avoid the classic RPG problem of finding fifteen enraged wolves waiting on a road for twenty years without eating absolutely anything.
3. Important Rule: Creature Does Not Mean Enemy

Historical documentation groups very different beings under “Enemies,” including creatures, intelligent individuals, and even members of organizations such as Writers or Shinigami. The current World Bible must separate these categories.
This distinction is important so that the Bestiary does not end up classifying a Ministry official among “aggressive fungi and dragons.”
For production, I would use seven categories, even though the original template proposed five.
An especially important rule: Not every Boss represents a species.

After years of abandonment, energy residues accumulated. From those remains emerged: Arz. Goetia
described as a creature composed of waste from pure elemental energy, Chaos, pain, and destruction.
It has no natural habitat. Its existence is tied to the laboratory that accidentally produced it.
It cannot be domesticated and is not part of a normal ecological chain. It is magical contamination turned into an organism.
Its presence demonstrates that poorly managed magic can produce dangerous artificial ecosystems. This idea is extremely useful for the world.

An important question for this universe: can a creature disappear forever?
If Will and magic exist, this must be resolved carefully. My recommendation: the existence of magic should not make extinction impossible. Otherwise, preserving ecosystems loses much of its meaning.
Will opens a particular possibility: sufficiently intense events may leave behind forms of life or entities.

This allows us to create creatures whose origin is truly unique to the world. A battle lasting one hundred years leaves so much residual Will that abandoned weapons begin to manifest behaviors of their own.
That would be much more interesting than: “magical monster number 37.”
